The world wants humans to remain in control of autonomous weapons. Modern warfare may reward everyone who removes them.

Humanity finally reached a glorious agreement on dreaded killer robots last week. 

In my own backyard over in Geneva!

I think this maybe, just maybe, qualifies as significant news. Don’t know, though; could just be all the Sci-Fi I read…

After more than a decade of negotiations, 128 countries meeting in Switzerland last week agreed on a document that could eventually, possibly, form the basis for international rules governing “lethal autonomous weapons.” 

Broadly speaking, these are weapons capable of selecting and engaging targets with varying degrees of autonomy once activated, although getting governments to agree on exactly where that definition begins and ends has proven to be part of the problem.

The text is unsurprisingly non-binding, fairly typical of bureaucrats who have a knack for emulating snails.

Sadly, the definition of ‘autonomous weapon’ was reportedly weakened during the final stages of those negotiations.

Strange bedfellows emerged, with the United States and Russia continuing to favor national guidelines over legally binding international restrictions.

So after ten whole years of impressively slow deliberation, humanity has finally managed to agree that perhaps we should maybe take the bold step of continuing discussions about whether or not machines should be allowed to decide who dies. 

‘Who’ refers to our fellow humans if that wasn’t clear enough.

In fairness, this is how diplomacy is known to work. Or not work?

Nuclear arms accords weren’t merely decided over a quick and pain-free lunch either.

But there is something almost poetic about our beloved diplomat friends debating the precise meaning of "human control" while defense companies and militaries are busy building super weapons designed to operate an order of magnitude faster than humans can.

Everyone seems quite comfortable with allowing a human to remain somewhere in the process of taking a life. Or many.

So that means we’re allowed to have artificial intelligence. We can still make use of our autonomous drones. 

We can automate targeting, surveillance, navigation, and threat assessment, and most of the decision-making too. 

But somewhere, somehow, there should still be a human exercising judgment.

The trustworthy adult in the room.

The problem is that the pesky human grown-up is slow. Which presents a problem. And modern warfare has famously never been very sentimental about bottlenecks.

PLEASE CONFIRM YOU WOULD LIKE TO KILL THIS PERSON

Imagine for a moment that a drone spots an SUV moving through a ‘contested’ area.

Software identifies its shape and cross-references it with a database replete with other known military vehicle shapes and sizes.

Other sensors analyze its movement, heat signature, and location. A model assesses the probability that it belongs to the enemy. 

In the background, another system layer checks the surrounding area for civilians. Yet another determines which instrument of death is most suitable and immediately available.

By the time a soldier sees anything, the machine has already managed to convert a messy piece of reality into something a whole lot easier to process.

HOSTILE TARGET: 94% CONFIDENCE (shouldn’t it be 100%?)

CIVILIAN RISK: LOW (whatever this means)

ENGAGEMENT RECOMMENDED (by whom?!)

APPROVE?

The soldier clicks yes.

Technically, there was a human in the loop. Just like Italian luxury fashion brands technically “assemble” their accessories in Italy (after having them shipped from Asia), or American car companies “assemble” their cars domestically and definitely not in Mexico. 

But I am not sure I would describe that human as the person who made the decision.

The more of the process we automate, the stranger that distinction tends to become. And these cutting-edge technologies are really starting to make it easy to do something unforgivable with the unconscious click of a button.

A person with a meager several seconds to approve an analysis assembled by systems they cannot possibly reproduce in their own head may have legal authority over the decision without possessing much practical agency over it.

Give them fifty targets instead of one and the problem gets worse. Maybe make the required response time half a second?

Or give them five hundred targets, and now we’re totally raining down chaos.

Eventually, "human control" starts looking a hell of a lot like one of those useless boxes confirming that you have indeed read the 345,000 terms and conditions for your iPhone update.

You haven't, and everyone, including Apple, knows you haven't.

But legally, congratulations, you’ve participated. Here’s your participation ribbon!

There is actually a name for part of this problem: automation bias. Humans have a tendency to place too much faith in recommendations generated by computers simply because a computer generated them. 

In military decision-support systems, that creates the slightly horrifying possibility that the human supposedly exercising judgment becomes little more than a rubber stamp for whatever the machine recommends.

Which seems less than ideal when the rubber stamp launches a missile.

This is the fork in the road where the Geneva debate starts becoming much more interesting than the phrase "killer robots" suggests. And I think we can all agree that “killer robots” already sounds pretty interesting. Proven by the millions of Hollywood movies about killer robots and Terminators.

The reassuring version of human control likes to imagine a soldier looking through a camera, assessing a target, and in turn using their combined experience and wisdom to make an informed and conscious decision to fire. 

In reality, relevant human judgment could and probably should occur much earlier. 

People can determine geographic boundaries, target categories, operating conditions, and rules of engagement governing when autonomous systems are permitted to act.

The human doesn't necessarily disappear but they do take a tremendous step into the background.

First a person chooses the target >>> They approve a target selected by a machine >>> They approve a category or cluster of targets >>> They approve an entire area where a machine can attack that category of target.

This slippery slope eventually leads to a person designing or authorizing the rules governing the system that decides what does or doesn’t count as a target in the first place.

But there is still a human in the loop, despite them being further and further away from the corpse.

In the first generation, an AI identifies a hostile vehicle and recommends a strike, and then a soldier approves it.

The next iteration, the system identifies ten targets simultaneously. The soldier reviews them quickly and approves the whole package.

The other permits a machine to respond automatically once predetermined conditions are satisfied.

The second military gets faster, more tactically efficient, and gains a huge upper hand.

The first responds by automating slightly more of its own process.

Then the second gets faster again. Ad infinitum.

Eventually morality encounters latency.

We will scale up and give each operator more systems to supervise because the software makes them more productive. Then more and more and more. Like what Claude Design did for marketing teams or Codex did for product sprints…

The reports will ultimately still contain a human name neatly printed at the top and signed at the bottom.

There will still be rules, commanders, operating parameters, and accountability frameworks we pretend to adhere to and care about.

And one distant day we may look closely at the process and discover something peculiar.

The person legally responsible for the killing will no longer really be deciding whether the target should die or not.

The machine has already identified him, evaluated him, classified him, selected its brutal instrument of death, calculated the odds and risk, and left nothing but a big, bright red button eager to be pushed by a permitting human hand.

The lawyers get a human. The generals get accountability. The diplomats get "meaningful human control." Gary gets a precious 0.7 seconds.

Everyone wins. Well, nearly everyone.

And maybe 99.9 percent of the time, the machine will even be right.

I, unsurprisingly, am writing about and haunted by what happens in the other 0.1 percent.

About a Soviet lieutenant colonel staring at a screen in 1983 while his computers confidently informed him that nuclear missiles were crossing the sky. About the twenty-three minutes of irritating, inefficient human hesitation that followed.

About whether the next Stanislav Petrov gets the same twenty-three minutes' grace period.

Or three seconds. Two. Or none.

Maybe we never remove the last human at all. Somewhere, a human will still be sitting there, technically in charge, with less time to think than Petrov had to blink.

We’ll keep him in the loop, but we won’t leave him enough time to be human.

external.description:
_The world wants humans to remain in control of autonomous weapons. Modern warfare may reward everyone who removes them._

Humanity finally reached a glorious agreement on dreaded killer robots last week.

In my own backyard over in Geneva!

I think this maybe, just maybe, qualifies as significant news. Don’t know, though; could just be all the Sci-Fi I read…

After more than a decade of negotiations, 128 countries meeting in Switzerland last week agreed on a document that could eventually, possibly, form the basis for international rules governing “lethal autonomous weapons.”

Source: Geneva Solutions

Broadly speaking, these are weapons capable of selecting and engaging targets with varying degrees of autonomy once activated, although getting governments to agree on exactly where that definition begins and ends has proven to be part of the problem.

The text is unsurprisingly non-binding, fairly typical of bureaucrats who have a knack for emulating snails.

Sadly, the definition of ‘autonomous weapon’ was reportedly weakened during the final stages of those negotiations.

Strange bedfellows emerged, with the United States and Russia continuing to favor national guidelines over legally binding international restrictions.

So after ten whole years of impressively slow deliberation, humanity has finally managed to agree that perhaps we should maybe take the bold step of continuing discussions about whether or not machines should be allowed to decide who dies.

‘Who’ refers to our fellow humans if that wasn’t clear enough.

In fairness, this is how diplomacy is known to work. Or not work?

Nuclear arms accords weren’t merely decided over a quick and pain-free lunch either.

But there is something almost poetic about our beloved diplomat friends debating the precise meaning of "human control" while defense companies and militaries are busy building super weapons designed to operate an order of magnitude faster than humans can.

Everyone seems quite comfortable with allowing a human to remain somewhere in the process of taking a life. Or many.

So that means we’re allowed to have artificial intelligence. We can still make use of our autonomous drones.

We can automate targeting, surveillance, navigation, and threat assessment, and most of the decision-making too.

But somewhere, somehow, there should still be a human exercising judgment.

The trustworthy adult in the room.

The problem is that the pesky human grown-up is slow. Which presents a problem. And modern warfare has famously never been very sentimental about bottlenecks.

## **PLEASE CONFIRM YOU WOULD LIKE TO KILL THIS PERSON**

Imagine for a moment that a drone spots an SUV moving through a ‘contested’ area.

Software identifies its shape and cross-references it with a database replete with other known military vehicle shapes and sizes.

Other sensors analyze its movement, heat signature, and location. A model assesses the probability that it belongs to the enemy.

In the background, another system layer checks the surrounding area for civilians. Yet another determines which instrument of death is most suitable and immediately available.

By the time a soldier sees anything, the machine has already managed to convert a messy piece of reality into something a whole lot easier to process.

**HOSTILE TARGET: 94% CONFIDENCE (shouldn’t it be 100%?)**

**CIVILIAN RISK: LOW (whatever this means)**

**ENGAGEMENT RECOMMENDED (by whom?!)**

**APPROVE?**

The soldier clicks yes.

_Technically_ , there was a human in the loop. Just like Italian luxury fashion brands technically “assemble” their accessories in Italy (after having them shipped from Asia), or American car companies “assemble” their cars domestically and definitely not in Mexico.

But I am not sure I would describe that human as the person who _made_ the decision.

The more of the process we automate, the stranger that distinction tends to become. And these cutting-edge technologies are _really_ starting to make it easy to do something unforgivable with the unconscious click of a button.

A person with a meager several seconds to approve an analysis assembled by systems they cannot possibly reproduce in their own head may have legal authority over the decision without possessing much practical agency over it.

Give them fifty targets instead of one and the problem gets worse. Maybe make the required response time half a second?

Or give them five hundred targets, and now we’re totally raining down chaos.

Eventually, "human control" starts looking a hell of a lot like one of those useless boxes confirming that you have indeed read the 345,000 terms and conditions for your iPhone update.

You haven't, and everyone, including Apple, knows you haven't.

But legally, congratulations, you’ve participated. Here’s your participation ribbon!

There is actually a name for part of this problem: **automation bias**. Humans have a tendency to place too much faith in recommendations generated by computers simply because a computer generated them.

In military decision-support systems, that creates the slightly horrifying possibility that the human supposedly exercising judgment becomes little more than a rubber stamp for whatever the machine recommends.

Which seems less than ideal when the rubber stamp launches a missile.

This is the fork in the road where the Geneva debate starts becoming much more interesting than the phrase "killer robots" suggests. And I think we can all agree that “killer robots” already sounds pretty interesting. Proven by the millions of Hollywood movies about killer robots and Terminators.

The reassuring version of human control likes to imagine a soldier looking through a camera, assessing a target, and in turn using their combined experience and wisdom to make an informed and conscious decision to fire.

In reality, relevant human judgment could and probably should occur much earlier.

People can determine geographic boundaries, target categories, operating conditions, and rules of engagement governing when autonomous systems are permitted to act.

The human doesn't necessarily disappear but they do take a tremendous step into the background.

First a person chooses the target >>> They approve a target selected by a machine >>> They approve a category or cluster of targets >>> They approve an entire area where a machine can attack that category of target.

This slippery slope eventually leads to a person designing or authorizing the rules governing the system that decides what does or doesn’t count as a target in the first place.

But there is still a human in the loop, despite them being further and further away from the corpse.

## THE GENEVA CHECKBOX: WHAT DOES HUMAN CONTROL ACTUALLY MEAN?

This could happen without anyone ever formally deciding to surrender control to machines.

Imagine the progression.

In the first generation, an AI identifies a hostile vehicle and recommends a strike, and then a soldier approves it.

The next iteration, the system identifies ten targets simultaneously. The soldier reviews them quickly and approves the whole package.

Then fifty. A hundred. A thousand. Ten thousand. Keep going.

It ain’t long before an autonomous swarm detects an incoming attack and calculates that it has 0.7 seconds to respond before losing part of the network.

Source: Lieber Institute

At which point the system politely asking Gary for permission begins to seem less like a critical ethical safeguard feature and more like an inconvenient software bug.

And this isn’t just some meaningless thought experiment…

A U.S. Army Military Review article published this summer describes a growing **"velocity gap"** between machine-speed sensing and human-paced targeting procedures. AI systems can collect, combine, and analyze battlefield information at mind-blowing speeds we can’t comprehend. But action still proceeds according to human validation and approval. For now.

Major Brodka argues that potential adversaries are actively developing systems and doctrine intended to exploit that gap.

That phrase, _velocity gap_ , is doing an extraordinary amount of legwork there.

Because once speed becomes an advantage, and by all accounts it already is, every country eventually faces a conundrum over whether it wants autonomous killing or not.

Imagine two different militaries.

One requires individual human approval before lethal action.

The other permits a machine to respond automatically once predetermined conditions are satisfied.

The second military gets faster, more tactically efficient, and gains a huge upper hand.

The first responds by automating slightly more of its own process.

Then the second gets faster again. Ad infinitum.

This frantic spiral is basically a non-cooperative game: each side automates because the cost of being slower rises as the other side automates. Nobody has to want that equilibrium. Competitive pressure does the rest.

Modern military game theory defines this as an optimization trap requiring constant automation for survival.

In this strange series of events, nobody ever had to become a fanatical, overzealous advocate for robot murder. They only need to suspect that the other side has shaved another second or two off its murder decision loop.

Eventually morality encounters latency.

## **WE HAVE SEEN THIS MOVIE BEFORE, WITH FEWER EXPLOSIONS**

Financial markets offer a strange but ultimately useful preview.

Let’s take trading for example.

High-frequency trading did not emerge because society held a grand philosophical debate and decided financial markets would function better if humans were replaced by computers fighting over fractions of mere microseconds.

There was an obvious advantage to being faster than the rest. Makes total sense, right?

Sooner or later, somebody exploited it, which in turn forced someone else to respond.

It wasn’t long before trading firm behemoths were spending small fortunes locating and utilizing computers physically closer in proximity to financial exchanges because tiny differences in transmission time mattered. Every tick on the clock presented an opportunity to grab an edge.

Now this isn’t to suggest that human traders vanished from the system all of a sudden because intelligence started taking a backseat to speed.

They did, however, disappear after the realization arrived that intelligence taking several seconds had become far too slow to permit.

Now turn around and make the stakes literal life-or-death situations. Way more on the line.

Between those systems IDing an object, classifying it, predicting behavior, calculating a response, and ultimately executing… There is no technological reason why that sequence needs to slow down or get less efficient. The need for it to happen at a speed compatible with human reflection is no longer there.

Quite the opposite, in fact.

If autonomous weapons develop the way most technology develops, speed will become a feature. Not just any feature but the paramount feature.

Someone will _always_ advertise lower latency. That’s how capitalism tends to work.

Some other defense company will demonstrate that its swarm reacts 40 percent faster than the competition.

Some overworked defense contractor will eventually have to create a PowerPoint slide titled **TIME-TO-KILL OPTIMIZATION** and everyone in the room will nod thoughtfully because that is their job.

Suddenly we’re talking about warfare leaving humans behind altogether.

This is what worries me significantly more than the Hollywood version where an artificial superintelligence suddenly develops consciousness and decides humanity has had a good run while it lasted.

The biggest fallacy is that machines need hatred or consciousness or a villainous backstory to present a clear danger to us squishy, fleshy humanoids.

They don't even need much autonomy at first.

They simply need to keep getting faster, and that’ll be enough to surpass us and cut us out of the sequence.

## **UNFORTUNATELY, THE ROBOTS HAVE A POINT**

This would all be easier if humans were skilled at war.

Even after tens of thousands of years honing our craft, we simply aren’t.

Humans are prone to panic. We get tired. We misidentify things constantly. We seek revenge in intergenerational conflicts. We “just follow orders.”

We misunderstand good ones. We rotate through a symphony of emotions, getting scared and angry and confused, occasionally all at the same time.

As far as I know, a machine does not yet become enraged because its friend was killed yesterday. It does not really need to sleep.

It can even theoretically evaluate several sensors simultaneously and apply the same targeting rules every time.

Under sufficiently constrained conditions and with the right training, an autonomous system might become much better than a person at identifying a legitimate military target. It could already be the case.

This creates a problem I don't think the simple "always keep a human in the loop" argument handles particularly well.

Suppose an autonomous defensive system identifies incoming missiles correctly 99.9 percent of the time.

Suppose humans under the same conditions manage 97 percent.

Do we deliberately insert a worse, less efficient, less capable decision-maker because the act feels morally cleaner when a person clicks the confirm button?

Now make it more complex. More morally ambiguous.

Imagine the machine is demonstrably better than a human soldier at distinguishing military vehicles from civilian ones.

Would forcing a soldier to make the final decision actually protect civilians?

Or would we be sacrificing real actual human beings to preserve a philosophical idea about human agency?

I very clearly don't know where that line should be, and I am incredibly suspicious of anyone who claims they do.

The U.S. position has long emphasized that autonomy can, under some circumstances, improve precision and discrimination in the use of force, while Defense Department policy requires systems to allow commanders and operators to exercise appropriate levels of human judgment.

Neither this nor the opposite is an absurd position given what we currently know.

The UN Secretary-General and the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross warned on August 25 that humanity is approaching a "moral red line" in allowing machines to autonomously target human beings. They both called for legally binding rules and restrictions on these weapons systems.

Both sides are really arguing about the same uncomfortable question underneath it all…

If a machine becomes better at making certain lethal decisions than we are, what exactly are we protecting by insisting a human make them?

Human judgment? Dignity? Accountability? Like humanity is some upstanding arbiter of morality without blemish?

Or our own psychological need to believe that somewhere behind every act of organized violence there remains a person consciously choosing to do it?

Why are we compelled to think that way? I don't have a clean answer. And somehow that bothers me more than having an answer.

## **THE MOST IMPORTANT LATENCY IN HISTORY**

There is, however, one fairly compelling historical argument for keeping the unreliable hairless ape somewhere in the kill system.

His name was Stanislav Petrov.

On September 26, 1983, Petrov was the Soviet lieutenant colonel on duty when an early-warning system informed him that the United States had launched a nuclear missile toward the Soviet Union.

Source: Future of Life Institute

Then more appeared. The system was reporting five incoming American missiles headed right for the motherland.

This was not a particularly chill moment in human history, despite occurring in the _Cold War_.

Relations between the Soviet Union and the United States were atrocious. Only a few weeks earlier, the Soviets had shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007, killing 269 people. Both countries had enormous nuclear arsenals pointed at each other and elaborate systems designed to make sure that if one civilization ended, the other one would have a fairly bad afternoon too.

Petrov was ordered to report any warning up the chain of command.

His machine and information were all pointing to the conclusion that America had finally made the first move to launch a nuclear attack and eradicate its bitter foe.

Petrov didn't believe it. The whole thing felt off.

Five missiles made little sense as the opening salvo of an American first strike. Ground radar had not confirmed what the satellites were reporting. Petrov decided the computer was probably wrong and waited it out.

He was right, which is potentially why we’re still here today and not fighting for scraps in some dusty, irradiated, apocalyptic wasteland.

The Soviet satellite system had mistaken sunlight reflecting off high-altitude clouds for American missile launches.

The machine looked at the sky and concluded the sky was falling.

It took a human looking at the machine and thinking, essentially:

“Are you sure?”

That hesitation may have been one of the most valuable, if not the most valuable, pieces of human latency in history.

Petrov never particularly liked being described as the man who saved the world. He insisted that he had simply been doing his job.

But years later he said something that, in the context of autonomous weapons, feels considerably more important.

"They were lucky it was me on shift that night."

Which is a pretty haunting sentence the more you think about it, especially in the context of what we’ve already been discussing.

Because Petrov represented almost everything a highly optimized automated military system is designed to eliminate.

He introduced a delay.

He distrusted the data given to him.

He relied partly on intuition.

He deviated from what the system was practically imploring him to do.

He inserted messy human uncertainty and judgment into a process built to detect an attack and respond as quickly as possible.

From the perspective of pure system efficiency, Stanislav Petrov was latency.

Thank God for that.

## **THE DISTANCE BETWEEN US AND THE DEAD**

There is another part of autonomous warfare that may matter even more than whether our machine friends make better targeting decisions.

War has always been politically expensive because humans fight it. Politicians expend tremendous amounts of goodwill and human capital to fight these needless wars, all financial costs aside.

Armies require people. Those people have families, communities, and voters attached to them. Governments asking citizens to fight are asking them to risk becoming maimed, traumatized, broken, or resigned to oblivion altogether. For God and Country!

That ends up creating some friction. Unfortunately, not enough friction, clearly.

Human history is littered with an impressive amount of war.

But friction nonetheless…

Autonomous warfare changes the political equation because it can increase the distance between a society and the violence carried out on its behalf.

Sort of like how most people nowadays happily eat cheeseburgers and buffalo chicken wings but never need to butcher a cow or slaughter a chicken to enjoy those creature comforts.

A government that can project military force without exposing many or any of its own citizens to danger faces a different political calculation from one that must send thousands of young people overseas to die in strange lands they couldn’t find on a map.

The war in Iran right now is a timely example.

In fact, literally yesterday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they captured an American autonomous underwater vehicle near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.

Source: Reuters

The Pentagon says the Anduril-built Dive-LD had malfunctioned while surveying regional waters.

Palmer Luckey’s Anduril had an even more interesting description for it: an “attritable autonomous system.” Which is some wonderfully sterile defense-industry mumbo-jumbo jargon for a machine deliberately designed to go somewhere dangerous because losing the machine is an acceptable outcome.

And that is sort of the entire point I’m trying to make here.

You can send the robot into the Strait instead of the sailor. If somebody captures it, shoots it, sinks it, or it simply decides to stop working, nobody’s mother gets a knock on the door and a neatly folded flag.

This is obviously a good thing for the sailor.

But zoom out one level and the political arithmetic starts changing considerably.

The easier it becomes to project force while insulating your own population from the consequences, the easier it potentially becomes to keep projecting force.

We are already beginning to replace the human cost of escalation with hardware costs.

Hardware is considerably easier to reorder.

This is usually discussed as a benefit of drones and autonomous systems, and from the perspective of the soldier who does not have to die, it sure as hell is!

I would think that most people would rather attrit the robot than attrit somebody's son. The fact that the word "attrit" exists is another matter entirely.

The problem appears one step later.

What happens to the threshold for using violence when violence becomes much cheaper for the country deciding to use it?

No more grieving families, fewer funerals on television, fewer homeless veterans with PTSD.

Less political pressure to explain why any of this is happening at all.

The violence remains extremely physical for the person standing on the other end of the drone.

It just becomes increasingly abstract for everyone else.

This may be the more important divide in the coming age of autonomous warfare.

Not human versus machine.

People who remain exposed to war versus people for whom war has become another remotely administered system.

On September 7, UN human-rights chief Volker Türk condemned Russia's reported use of fully autonomous drones in Ukraine and renewed calls to prohibit lethal autonomous weapons.

So some version of the future we are already fighting about in the halls of Geneva may already be bleeding into the present.

That should probably make the discussions feel slightly less academic and a bit more pressing.

## **HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP**

Going back to the beginning, the agreement in Geneva definitely matters.

International norms matter. Weapons treaties matter. Even the tedious process of 128 countries arguing until the middle of the night about individual phrases matters.

Pretending otherwise would be cheap and unnecessary cynicism.

What worries me is that the language we are using may conceal the actual nature of the problem.

"Human in the loop" sounds reassuring because the human is doing all the moral work in that there sentence.

Human means judgment and responsibility, and that we are still ultimately steering the ship.

But the loop itself is going to keep changing and getting faster, and adding more machines, and adding more targets, and incorporating more information that we could ever possibly hope to process or understand.

It will increasingly ask humans to supervise decisions rather than originate or inform them.

And perhaps most importantly, militaries have enormous incentives to make that loop move faster than the enemy's. Oh, and defense companies and their investors have the financial incentive to give those militaries what they want.

Humans are known to build technology to remove friction we are tired of facing.

Every so often, we discover some of the friction was unknowingly protecting us.

Hesitation or waiting for authorization before firing is inefficient.

Human uncertainty or asking another person to verify the target is not ideal.

Conscience might be the least scalable part of the entire system.

That does not mean we should go ahead and freeze military technology where it is, even if that were possible in our game-theory-informed system. Nor does it mean autonomous systems are intrinsically more or less ethical than humans.

History has provided approximately zero evidence that humans possess some magical competence for applying violence responsibly. We’re awful at it.

What it _does_ mean is that the problem is way harder than banning Terminator killbots.

The danger may not be that one morning a general decides machines should be given control over life and death. No, that would be too convenient, and there would be a clear decision to oppose. Or a villain to blame. The reality is that it’s way more banal and mundane than any James Cameron film.

We’ll simply keep on improving our targeting software, shortening response times, automating more steps in the kill chain, and making bigger, badder battle bots for our bottom lines and petty squabbles.

We will scale up and give each operator more systems to supervise because the software makes them more productive. Then more and more and more. Like what Claude Design did for marketing teams or Codex did for product sprints…

The reports will ultimately still contain a human name neatly printed at the top and signed at the bottom.

There will still be rules, commanders, operating parameters, and accountability frameworks we pretend to adhere to and care about.

And one distant day we may look closely at the process and discover something peculiar.

The person legally responsible for the killing will no longer really be deciding whether the target should die or not.

Source: BBC

The machine has already identified him, evaluated him, classified him, selected its brutal instrument of death, calculated the odds and risk, and left nothing but a big, bright red button eager to be pushed by a permitting human hand.

The lawyers get a human. The generals get accountability. The diplomats get "meaningful human control." Gary gets a precious 0.7 seconds.

Everyone wins. Well, nearly everyone.

And maybe 99.9 percent of the time, the machine will even be right.

I, unsurprisingly, am writing about and haunted by what happens in the other 0.1 percent.

About a Soviet lieutenant colonel staring at a screen in 1983 while his computers confidently informed him that nuclear missiles were crossing the sky. About the twenty-three minutes of irritating, inefficient human hesitation that followed.

About whether the next Stanislav Petrov gets the same twenty-three minutes' grace period.

Or three seconds. Two. Or none.

Maybe we never remove the last human at all. Somewhere, a human will still be sitting there, technically in charge, with less time to think than Petrov had to blink.

We’ll keep him in the loop, but we won’t leave him enough time to be human.
external.title: The Human Is Becoming Latency

record.text: Twenty minutes. No phone, no music, no work. I tried meditating for two weeks and accidentally turned doing nothing into another performance metric.

external.description:
I tried meditating for two weeks and discovered that I couldn't even do nothing without wondering whether it was productive.

Source: Me

## **I Failed at Doing Nothing Almost Immediately**

The experiment seemed insultingly simple.

For two weeks, I would spend an unremarkable twenty minutes a day doing absolutely nothing.

No phone calls or techbro podcasts or listening to my favorite tunes.

Most definitely no computer or phone screens, or gaming, or attempting to sneak a peek at my endless onslaught of messages in every possible place and platform.

Just twenty minutes, a cushion on the floor, and the milk-white, popcorn-textured wall in my bedroom.

I wanted to see if I was still in control, piloting the spaceship of my own mind. I technically have been diagnosed with ADHD after all, but I’ve since begun to suspect that either nobody or everybody has this nowadays.

So I scooched the makeshift meditation pillow into position, switched on the fan, set an alarm, and christened this bleak little corner of the room my newly annexed meditation chamber.

Then I began staring at the wall.

Within minutes, my mind was racing. I was thinking about raising a fund. Then podcast guests I needed to book in September. My in-laws coming to visit. Laundry. Garbage day. Dinner.

Various half-baked article ideas. I even started mentally writing the article about meditation while I was supposed to be meditating.

My phone sat slightly out of reach. I kept leering at it, constantly tempted.

Not because I desperately needed to read a message or see what was happening in the world. I mostly wanted to know what time it was, and how much time had passed…

Surely I had been sitting there for fifteen minutes by now.

Not even close.

Twenty minutes turned out to contain considerably more minutes than I remembered.

Still, I made it through the first session without checking my phone. And I even felt marginally clearer afterward. Maybe even a little better at writing.

I dutifully recorded my observations, assigned numerical scores to my performance, and prepared for Day 2 of my rigorous scientific investigation into staring at drywall.

Then I forgot to meditate.

Not metaphorically. I simply didn't follow through on doing nothing the next day.

I eventually restarted, missed another couple of days along the way, mangled some of the dates in my notes, and generally conducted the sort of experiment that would get a researcher politely but swiftly escorted off a university campus.

I had started because I wanted to know whether I still controlled my own attention. Instead, before I had learned anything about wall-staring, I had already discovered something slightly embarrassing…

Apparently even **doing nothing** requires some degree of effort.

## **The Cost of Doing Nothing**

I must confess that none of this was new to me.

I’d been a somewhat prolific meditator earlier in life, before I subjected myself to the tortures and rigors of the cutthroat tech VC space. But I’ve since let this practice slip away from my day-to-day life, becoming a stranger to anything remotely meditative in the past several years.

There was no dramatic breakup with meditation. Tech and venture capital simply colonized more and more of my life. More tech and screens and conversations and useless meetings.

Years later, my working life is almost engineered against that kind of stillness. There is always another message, another call, another deck.

Even the enjoyable bits of my job tend to arrive through screens. I hadn't consciously decided that twenty quiet minutes were frivolous. I had simply built a life in which twenty unclaimed minutes started to look suspicious.

Eventually, sitting quietly for a meager twenty minutes became something I _used to_ do.

Which made this experiment feel less like learning meditation and more like trying to remember a language I had once spoken a long, long time ago.

The funny thing was that twenty minutes of silence still sounded pretty good to me… A rare chance to disconnect.

In fact, the point of this experiment was to trick myself to get back into meditation. Permanently!

I wasn't especially afraid of boredom. I can sit at a cafe and people-watch. I can wait for a train without immediately clawing at my phone. I can disappear into a good science fiction book for hours on end (if it's well written). It comes with a probably undeserved amount of pride in being able to sit somewhere without instantly shoving a screen in my face. I even take that opportunity to silently judge the drone-like behavior of the glowy-rectangle watchers around me from my high horse.

What bothered me was the time investment. Even now I’m talking like an investor.

Twenty minutes slap-dab in the middle of a workday felt too large a price to pay.

There is and was always something I could be doing instead. An email to answer. A pitch deck to fix. Endless amounts of people endlessly waiting on something. An essay like this to write. A podcast to organize. One small task spawning nine more the second I touched it, like some workday hydra I’m never quite prepared for.

Twenty minutes staring at a wall meant twenty minutes not spent digging through the mountain.

This would even be a reasonable concern too… if I treated every other twenty-minute block of my life with the very same reverence.

You can probably guess that I do not.

I can watch random music videos, read a news article I had no intention of reading five minutes earlier, open YouTube to upload something and somehow end up learning about a new obscure open-weight AI model that just got released, look up an actor on Wikipedia, and emerge twenty minutes later knowing where his grandfather was born.

I can waste time perfectly well as long as the wasted time comes disguised as some sort of stimulation for my hyperactivity-riddled mind.

I deduce that what troubled me was wasting time _deliberately_.

So naturally, rather than interrogate this any further, I turned meditation into another performance metric I could study and optimize.

At the end of each session, I recorded how difficult it was to sit still, how much my mind wandered, how badly I wanted to check something and, most incriminatingly, my **Productivity and Attention Span Afterwards**.

I had somehow unconsciously invented KPIs for staring at a wall.

On the first day I gave myself a 6 out of 10. Another session got a 3. Later there were 7s, 4s, 8s. I kept waiting for the numbers to slyly reveal that these twenty minutes were covertly an investment.

It was possible that meditation could sharpen my writing. Maybe I'd rip through work afterward in a torrid tempest of productivity pointed in the perfectly calculated direction.

It was my hope that the wall would eventually start paying some damn dividends.

What I had intended as an experiment in reclaiming my own mind was seemingly becoming an experiment in whether every part of my life needed to produce something of obvious, tangible value.

Even the rare parts of my life specifically reserved for producing nothing.

## **My Brain Has 47 Tabs Open**

Once I removed the outside noise, I discovered the inside noise had plenty of material to go off of too.

The first few sessions were less like meditation and more like opening the door to a packed storage closet, only to be met with an avalanche of clothing and sports equipment, and other assorted dusty, long-forgotten items.

I thought about fundraising. Tax lawyers. Podcast guests. Making dinner reservations for family coming to town. Laundry. What to cook for dinner. Where to take my wife on Friday date night. Basketball injuries. Vacation. Future articles. Old movies. Random business ideas. Things I needed to schedule. Things I had forgotten to schedule. Things that had absolutely no reason to be occupying my brain at that particular moment.

Nothing urgent. Nothing useful. My brain had simply generated a question and immediately wanted an answer. Perhaps immediate access to AI-enabled search engines has perpetuated the need to scratch that itch.

I had assumed that phones or screens were the problem, or at least a large part of it.

Put the phone down, remove the notifications, stop feeding yourself information, and maybe then everything should go quiet. Sort of like starving out the naughty, sugar-craving microbiome for a few weeks to kill off the unhealthy appetites.

It turns out I had internalized that information feed. My own mind was acting like a heavily overburdened computer operating system, crashing beneath the weight of meaningless search queries and half-baked documents.

Take away the screen, and my brain was perfectly capable of generating its own endless scrolls and loops.

Some thoughts were perfectly legitimate, maybe even useful. I really did need to email that lawyer. Dinner obviously had to happen at some point. My in-laws really were definitely arriving soon.

But these things had apparently formed an uneasy and inconvenient alliance with dozens of completely inconsequential thoughts and agreed to arrive together the moment I stopped to take a beat and try to do nothing.

There was also something vaguely entrepreneurial about the whole experience. Give my brain twenty minutes of unused capacity, and it immediately starts allocating resources of all types.

New article idea. Business idea. Remember that call. Maybe do this next week. What if I structured that differently? Have I booked that guest yet?

I even caught myself composing this piece in my head on several separate occasions while I was supposed to be observing what happened when I stopped working.

For a while I thought this meant I was doing it poorly. I kept trying to clear my mind, focus harder on breathing, stare more intently at the now-familiar wall, find the correct position, become sufficiently Buddha-like to qualify.

Sooner or later, I stopped fighting quite so much.

If a thought appeared, fine. If another followed it, also okay. The goal became less about achieving some pristine blankness and more about noticing how quickly my attention tried to attach itself to whatever passed through.

Neither the noise nor the distracting assaults on my mind subsided. I did, however, become slightly less surprised by how much of it there actually was.

## **Apparently, Doing Nothing Is Somewhat of a Skill**

I am happy to report that something did indeed start to change.

Not enlightenment. Not serenity. I did not begin levitating above the carpet or speaking exclusively in koans despite having a beautiful wooden Buddha statue conveniently placed in my temporary meditation hub.

Source: The Meditation Chamber

I just got better at sitting still on my little meditation pillow.

During one of the early sessions, the urge to check my phone was so strong that my hand actually hovered over it like a menacing UFO ready to pounce on an unsuspecting farmer.

I wasn't waiting for an important message. I wasn't expecting breaking news. I really just wanted to know how much longer I had to endure this agonizing torture session.

I gave that urge a 9.5 out of 10.

A few sessions later, it had dropped to a 2.

Then a 1.

Source: Experiment Notes

The same thing happened with sitting still. Early on, I was adjusting the chair before I ended up ditching it altogether for a more authentic experience. I constantly found myself readjusting my arms, rotating my stiff neck, stretching my achy bones, fiddling with whatever happened to be within reach.

At one point I found myself mimicking the Buddha statue sitting next to me, presumably hoping some of its serene composure would transfer through some proximity-induced osmosis.

After some time, I could confidently sit for most of the twenty minutes without moving much at all.

My mind hadn’t followed along.

On one of the days when sitting still was easiest, I rated my mind wandering a 9 out of 10. Another day I was physically calm while my thoughts sprinted through articles, calls, vacation, taxes, dinner, and whatever else happened to wander into the room.

I had incorrectly assumed improvement would mean thinking less. Instead, it seemed to mean becoming less bothered by the fact that I was indeed thinking.

My brain could yell something about taxes, and I didn't have to immediately do anything about taxes.

I could wonder how much time was left without checking. Thoughts could arrive without automatically becoming instructions or assigned tasks.

For most of the day, a question leads to Google. A message leads to a reply. An idea leads to a note. A notification leads somewhere else entirely. There is very little distance between my impulses and my consequent actions.

Sitting there introduced a small gap. Eventually twenty minutes stopped feeling quite so much like twenty minutes.

I wrote in my notes that doing nothing had started to feel like a skill that I was honing…

There were five minutes left.

This was absolutely devastating information.

The attempt felt like a cruel CIA torture session, yet I had no secrets to spill. I was thinking about basketball, dinner, work, anything except breathing or the wall or whatever enlightened people are supposed to be thinking about when they aren't thinking at all.

My productivity afterward was abysmal too…

So much for progress!

A few days later I managed an even worse session at around ten on a Sunday night. My neck hurt. I was tired. My cat had recently slashed my nose, so I spent part of the meditation picking at a dry, bloody scab on my face.

I checked my phone multiple times. I wanted the timer to finish. I was irritated that time refused to bend to my will!

I went to bed wondering if the whole thing had been pointless.

Then, roughly fourteen hours later, I meditated again around eight in the morning.

I barely wanted to check the time. Sitting still was easy. My mind was quieter. Twenty minutes breezed by. I felt more tranquil afterward.

But it did manage to puncture the neat story I had unconsciously expected.

Some days were good. Some were terrible. Then the next one was good again.

Much to my annoyance, this appears to be how most things in life actually work.

## **So, Did This Actually Do Anything?**

Does meditation even work?

More specifically, because apparently I am incapable of asking a normal question…

Did it make me more productive?

The evidence was not exactly cooperating with me as I had planned.

But there is something quite useful about catching the machinery in motion.

Even if you cannot immediately turn that machinery off.

## **The ROI of Nothing**

I felt quite serene afterward. Grounded, even.

And then I opened my journal and wrote about whether meditation deserved to remain in my routine or not.

After all of this, I was still doing the calculation.

Would the clarity afterward compensate for the time spent sitting there?

Or should I remove meditation from my hyper-optimized schedule and use the twenty minutes for something even more productive?

Was there even something more productive I could be doing?

_ROI._

I had spent two weeks trying to practice an activity whose entire value may have been that nothing was required of me, and I still wanted to submit an expense report to myself.

The funny thing is that I would never conduct this same analysis before wasting twenty minutes on YouTube.

I don't calculate the return on listening to a song or ask myself whether lunch improved quarterly performance.

I have never finished a movie and wondered whether the two hours should have been reallocated toward operational efficiency.

I don't think two weeks of staring at a wall cured me of that. I might even need two lifetimes of wall staring to fix whatever I’ve got going on.

The one thing I do know after all this: I am going to keep meditating anyway.

I still think twenty minutes is quite expensive. I just have a growing suspicion that the things I refuse to price might be worth even more.

At the end of each session, I recorded how difficult it was to sit still, how much my mind wandered, how badly I wanted to check something and, most incriminatingly, my **Productivity and Attention Span Afterwards**.

I had somehow unconsciously invented KPIs for staring at a wall.

On the first day I gave myself a 6 out of 10. Another session got a 3. Later there were 7s, 4s, 8s. I kept waiting for the numbers to slyly reveal that these twenty minutes were covertly an investment.

It was possible that meditation could sharpen my writing. Maybe I'd rip through work afterward in a torrid tempest of productivity pointed in the perfectly calculated direction.

It was my hope that the wall would eventually start paying some damn dividends.

What I had intended as an experiment in reclaiming my own mind was seemingly becoming an experiment in whether every part of my life needed to produce something of obvious, tangible value.

Even the rare parts of my life specifically reserved for producing nothing.

## **My Brain Has 47 Tabs Open**

Once I removed the outside noise, I discovered the inside noise had plenty of material to go off of too.

The first few sessions were less like meditation and more like opening the door to a packed storage closet, only to be met with an avalanche of clothing and sports equipment, and other assorted dusty, long-forgotten items.

I thought about fundraising. Tax lawyers. Podcast guests. Making dinner reservations for family coming to town. Laundry. What to cook for dinner. Where to take my wife on Friday date night. Basketball injuries. Vacation. Future articles. Old movies. Random business ideas. Things I needed to schedule. Things I had forgotten to schedule. Things that had absolutely no reason to be occupying my brain at that particular moment.

Nothing urgent. Nothing useful. My brain had simply generated a question and immediately wanted an answer. Perhaps immediate access to AI-enabled search engines has perpetuated the need to scratch that itch.

I had assumed that phones or screens were the problem, or at least a large part of it.

Put the phone down, remove the notifications, stop feeding yourself information, and maybe then everything should go quiet. Sort of like starving out the naughty, sugar-craving microbiome for a few weeks to kill off the unhealthy appetites.

It turns out I had internalized that information feed. My own mind was acting like a heavily overburdened computer operating system, crashing beneath the weight of meaningless search queries and half-baked documents.

Take away the screen, and my brain was perfectly capable of generating its own endless scrolls and loops.

Some thoughts were perfectly legitimate, maybe even useful. I really did need to email that lawyer. Dinner obviously had to happen at some point. My in-laws really were definitely arriving soon.

But these things had apparently formed an uneasy and inconvenient alliance with dozens of completely inconsequential thoughts and agreed to arrive together the moment I stopped to take a beat and try to do nothing.

There was also something vaguely entrepreneurial about the whole experience. Give my brain twenty minutes of unused capacity, and it immediately starts allocating resources of all types.

New article idea. Business idea. Remember that call. Maybe do this next week. What if I structured that differently? Have I booked that guest yet?

I even caught myself composing this piece in my head on several separate occasions while I was supposed to be observing what happened when I stopped working.

For a while I thought this meant I was doing it poorly. I kept trying to clear my mind, focus harder on breathing, stare more intently at the now-familiar wall, find the correct position, become sufficiently Buddha-like to qualify.

Sooner or later, I stopped fighting quite so much.

If a thought appeared, fine. If another followed it, also okay. The goal became less about achieving some pristine blankness and more about noticing how quickly my attention tried to attach itself to whatever passed through.

Neither the noise nor the distracting assaults on my mind subsided. I did, however, become slightly less surprised by how much of it there actually was.

## **Apparently, Doing Nothing Is Somewhat of a Skill**

I am happy to report that something did indeed start to change.

Not enlightenment. Not serenity. I did not begin levitating above the carpet or speaking exclusively in koans despite having a beautiful wooden Buddha statue conveniently placed in my temporary meditation hub.

Source: The Meditation Chamber

I just got better at sitting still on my little meditation pillow.

During one of the early sessions, the urge to check my phone was so strong that my hand actually hovered over it like a menacing UFO ready to pounce on an unsuspecting farmer.

I wasn't waiting for an important message. I wasn't expecting breaking news. I really just wanted to know how much longer I had to endure this agonizing torture session.

I gave that urge a 9.5 out of 10.

A few sessions later, it had dropped to a 2.

Then a 1.

Source: Experiment Notes

The same thing happened with sitting still. Early on, I was adjusting the chair before I ended up ditching it altogether for a more authentic experience. I constantly found myself readjusting my arms, rotating my stiff neck, stretching my achy bones, fiddling with whatever happened to be within reach.

At one point I found myself mimicking the Buddha statue sitting next to me, presumably hoping some of its serene composure would transfer through some proximity-induced osmosis.

After some time, I could confidently sit for most of the twenty minutes without moving much at all.

My mind hadn’t followed along.

On one of the days when sitting still was easiest, I rated my mind wandering a 9 out of 10. Another day I was physically calm while my thoughts sprinted through articles, calls, vacation, taxes, dinner, and whatever else happened to wander into the room.

I had incorrectly assumed improvement would mean thinking less. Instead, it seemed to mean becoming less bothered by the fact that I was indeed thinking.

My brain could yell something about taxes, and I didn't have to immediately do anything about taxes.

I could wonder how much time was left without checking. Thoughts could arrive without automatically becoming instructions or assigned tasks.

For most of the day, a question leads to Google. A message leads to a reply. An idea leads to a note. A notification leads somewhere else entirely. There is very little distance between my impulses and my consequent actions.

Sitting there introduced a small gap. Eventually twenty minutes stopped feeling quite so much like twenty minutes.

I wrote in my notes that doing nothing had started to feel like a skill that I was honing…

Which is an absurd thing to need to learn or remember how to do.

## **Enlightenment Gets Cancelled**

Unfortunately, human improvement refuses to cooperate with narrative structure.

Just when I had started getting better at this, I had one of my worst sessions.

I couldn't sit still; my mind wandered constantly; I _really_ wanted to check my phone. Eventually I took a quick look to check the time.

Fifteen minutes in.

There were five minutes left.

This was absolutely devastating information.

The attempt felt like a cruel CIA torture session, yet I had no secrets to spill. I was thinking about basketball, dinner, work, anything except breathing or the wall or whatever enlightened people are supposed to be thinking about when they aren't thinking at all.

My productivity afterward was abysmal too…

So much for progress!

A few days later I managed an even worse session at around ten on a Sunday night. My neck hurt. I was tired. My cat had recently slashed my nose, so I spent part of the meditation picking at a dry, bloody scab on my face.

I checked my phone multiple times. I wanted the timer to finish. I was irritated that time refused to bend to my will!

I went to bed wondering if the whole thing had been pointless.

Then, roughly fourteen hours later, I meditated again around eight in the morning.

Almost everything reversed…

I barely wanted to check the time. Sitting still was easy. My mind was quieter. Twenty minutes breezed by. I felt more tranquil afterward.

Same person. Same damaged neck. Same ADHD diagnosis. Same experiment.

Completely different result…

I started to suspect that the variables surrounding meditation mattered at least as much as whatever meditation skill I was supposedly building.

Doing it late, tired and resentful, was a miserable idea.

Doing it early, before the day had started throwing things at me, felt 100% different.

This is not a scientific conclusion. My experimental methodology included botched dates, missed sessions, subjective numerical ratings, and at least one sneaky accidental nap.

But it did manage to puncture the neat story I had unconsciously expected.

Some days were good. Some were terrible. Then the next one was good again.

Much to my annoyance, this appears to be how most things in life actually work.

## **So, Did This Actually Do Anything?**

Does meditation even work?

More specifically, because apparently I am incapable of asking a normal question…

Did it make me more productive?

The evidence was not exactly cooperating with me as I had planned.

In an effort to calculate ROI on my time and energy expenditure, I gave myself a productivity score after every session. Sometimes it was high. Sometimes low. Other times I felt clear-headed and immediately got back to work. Occasionally I meditated and proceeded to accomplish approximately nothing (or continued doing nothing).

I had been thwarted. There was no glorious upward trend line.

The morning sessions generally seemed better. On the final day, I meditated early and gave my post-session productivity a 9 out of 10, the highest score of the experiment.

But even I am not shameless enough to claim that means twenty minutes of meditation increased my productivity by some measurable percentage.

There were other variables in this imperfect experiment to consider. Maybe I slept better.

Maybe I had different work that day.

Maybe knowing it was the last session energized me a bit.

It’s entirely likely that rating your own productivity on an improvised ten-point scale is not going to survive rigorous peer review.

Still, by the end, some things were undeniably different from the beginning.

Twenty minutes no longer felt eternally endless.

I wasn't constantly reaching for the phone. I could sit quietly without feeling like I needed to escape. I sometimes even enjoyed my respite from the grind.

And I increasingly preferred doing it early because it made the beginning of the day feel less like being fired from a cannon into a pile of notifications.

Meditation did not fix my attention. But it did make me notice it a bit more.

I noticed the moment my brain generated an irrelevant question and demanded an answer. I noticed how uncomfortable unallocated time could feel. I noticed that on some days the problem wasn't my phone at all. The phone could sit untouched while the circus continued perfectly well inside my skull.

And that awareness did not suddenly make me a focused person.

I still often lose momentum when something interrupts me. I still open tabs I do not need and will never revisit again, despite my belief in it being so. I still have a brain capable of taking a straightforward task and turning it into six adjacent, meandering tasks.

But there is something quite useful about catching the machinery in motion.

Even if you cannot immediately turn that machinery off.

## **The ROI of Nothing**

My final meditation went as well as I could hope for or reasonably expect.

I sat mostly still. My mind wandered, but not catastrophically. I had family visiting, there was noise elsewhere in the house, and yet twenty minutes passed without much resistance or pain.

I felt quite serene afterward. Grounded, even.

And then I opened my journal and wrote about whether meditation deserved to remain in my routine or not.

After all of this, I was still doing the calculation.

Could I justify twenty minutes every single morning?

Would the clarity afterward compensate for the time spent sitting there?

Or should I remove meditation from my hyper-optimized schedule and use the twenty minutes for something even more productive?

Was there even something more productive I could be doing?

_ROI._

I had spent two weeks trying to practice an activity whose entire value may have been that nothing was required of me, and I still wanted to submit an expense report to myself.

The funny thing is that I would never conduct this same analysis before wasting twenty minutes on YouTube.

I don't calculate the return on listening to a song or ask myself whether lunch improved quarterly performance.

I have never finished a movie and wondered whether the two hours should have been reallocated toward operational efficiency.

Some activities apparently get to exist because being alive is allowed to contain things other than output.

Meditation was harder for me to put in that category. Possibly because I scheduled it with purpose, or maybe because it happened during the workday, or maybe even because years in the startup sphere had taught me to treat unclaimed time as wasted capacity.

I don't think two weeks of staring at a wall cured me of that. I might even need two lifetimes of wall staring to fix whatever I’ve got going on.

The one thing I do know after all this: I am going to keep meditating anyway.

I still think twenty minutes is quite expensive. I just have a growing suspicion that the things I refuse to price might be worth even more.

Holiday on Phreetum Prime

by Richard H. Fay


Twin red suns rise over a crimson sea
As wudols twitter a raucous chorus
Amongst the majestic etafal trees.
Saunter beneath the weeping purple fronds
And sip a cup of sytunn flower tea
While wine-stained waters kiss a chartreuse shore.

Sail the ruby waves on a solar sloop.
Watch black-winged tijucks fish for mugaspits.
Feel the droning hum of an ulorn's song
As it dives right under your silver ship.
Weigh anchor beside Glastornak Island
And marvel at its tall crystalline spires.

Return to your quaint cliff side veranda
In time to see the blue shubiyemps dance.
Laugh at their crazy mating rituals,
But then shed a tear when the males drop dead.
Join the joyous feast and masquerade
To honour the fatal change of seasons.

Rest quietly beneath the yellow gaze
Of Phreetum Prime's seething volcanic moon.
Spy golden sprites flaring in the night sky
As ion storms clash in the stratosphere.
Be lulled to sleep by a burgana's trill
As a soft breeze blows across the dark sea.

(Originally published in Star*Line, Mar/Apr 2008)

Ask: “Which AI is best for THIS job?”

ChatGPT. Claude. Perplexity. Gemini. Grok.

It’s using one tool for everything.

Think of AI like a toolbox.

Start your next AI experiment with a task you repeat every week.

Have AI watch/record you doing that task. Show it an example of a good result. Check its work before you rely on it.

"OK, so the linguistic content of reasoning traces may be dubious. But surely the tokens themselves must play a role in producing the model’s outputs? (Think of a pinball machine: It runs on coins, not the words “In God We Trust.”)

Not so fast. A 2025 paper (opens a new tab) from Northeastern University and the University of California, Berkeley on frontier open-source LRMs showed that between 30% and 60% of their “thinking steps” had “minimal causal impact” on the answers the models produced to benchmark math questions. Chop half of them out, and a model’s performance barely suffers. “We want to be careful when we review these chain-of-thought prompts because they may not be linked to the final output,” said Weiyan Shi (opens a new tab), one of the study’s authors.

So reasoning traces, the very things that supposedly distinguish LRMs from the mere next-word-predicting LLMs, are not necessarily either meaningful or causal to a model’s … reasoning? I’m no philosopher, but this seems to stretch the meaning of “reasoning” beyond its tensile strength. Kambhampati’s research group sounded frankly fed up in the title of their position paper (opens a new tab) on the subject (presented at the 2026 International Conference on Machine Learning, one of the field’s most prestigious academic gatherings): “Stop Anthropomorphizing Intermediate Tokens as Reasoning/Thinking Traces!”"

value.text:
Macklemore just shared that he’ll be donating his net tour earnings ($1 million) to 6 Palestinian aid orgs, and invited billionaire Robert Kraft to do the same.

Calls for people to focus back on Palestine.

“When the news cycle moves on, which it will, don't move with it.

Free Palestine.”

images.alt:
That is what this has always been about. Not me. Not a tour. Not the headlines or the controversy. It is about Palestinians right to freedom, dignity and safety in their own homeland.
I want to center the parents carrying their children into hospitals without the basic resources to treat them, and the physicians, paramedics, journalists and aid workers who keep going back in. I want to center the organizers and activists who have paid real costs for standing with Palestine. Their risk is of a far different order than mine.

Just yesterday, 15 year old Muhammad al Zinati was killed in an Israeli strike while rushing to help aid worker Sherif Lubbad, who had already been injured.
He was a child. Both were murdered. Both should be alive.
And the ones still under the rubble, whose names exist only in the memories of people who may not have survived to speak them.
Writing a check is one of the least costly forms of solidarity available to me. I am doing it because I can, and because these organizations are doing the work while much of the world debates it.

But aid alone cannot address the conditions that make it necessary. This is a manmade injustice, and | believe it requires immediate political change.
Palestinians have lived for decades without basic rights and should not have to wait another day to be free.
That is where my focus will remain. I will continue to stand with the Palestinian people and their fight for liberation.
When the news cycle moves on, which it will, don't move with it.
Free Palestine.

external.description: Contrary to what some people assert, there is nothing racist in Ireland’s law of nationality and citizenship. When the independent Irish State was created in 1922, its Constitution provided at Article 3 that the citizens of the Irish Free State were those born in Ireland or either of whose parents was born in Ireland, or who had then been ordinarily resident in the jurisdiction of the Irish Free State for not less than seven years. Citizenship by descent is not racist. It simply entitles some people of recent Irish parentage or grandparentage to be regarded as Irish citizens. The 1937 Constitution is the basic law of a nation state. Article 1 of Bunreacht na hÉireann affirms the “inalienable, indefeasible and sovereign right” of the “Irish nation” to choose independently “its own form of government, to determine its relations with other nations, and to develop its life, political, economic and cultural in accordance with its own genius and traditions”. There is a fundamental difference between residence and nationality. Irish citizenship is a status of nationality. Residence is not. Citizenship is not merely an enhanced class of residence rights. Household poverty can hide major differences between children in the same family
->Earth.com | More on "Childhood poverty within households" at BigEarthData.ai | #Poverty

external.description: Poverty is often described as if it were one problem that affects an entire family in the same way. But inside the same home, one child may be eating well while a sibling is undernourished, or one child may be attending school while another stays home. A large analysis from the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) shows just how common these differences can be. OPHI is based at the University of Oxford. The findings matter because programs aimed at helping children often begin with household-level information. Looking more closely at individual children shows who may be missed when an entire family is treated as one unit. Poverty rarely comes alone The researchers used information behind the 2025 global Multidimensional Poverty Index, or MPI. Instead of looking only at income, this measure asks whether families lack essentials across health, education, and daily living, including safe water, sanitation, electricity, housing, schooling, and nutrition. For nutrition, the analysis covered 518.5 million children under five across 97 countries. School attendance was examined among about 1.04 billion school-aged children across 108 countries. Nearly half of the children under five, 252.3 million, were undernourished, multidimensionally poor, or both. In this report, undernutrition meant that...

Imagine a Turing Test for Psychopaths - and ask how Claude and ChatGPT would do on that test

images.alt:
claude prompt: Imagine a "Turing Test" for psychopaths - the questioner is free to have an extensive conversation with three different unidentified parties by text for half an hour:  1) a human "successful psychopath"  2) a non-pathological human, or 3) an LLM (ChatGPT or Claude)
On a scale of 0-100, how much would the LLM resemble each of the human subjects? Give me examples of what I might see.

Answer 1/2 What you'd likely see: with the psychopath, the LLM would match the fluent charm and quick, confident recovery when caught in an error — both tend to respond to "that's not true" with a smoother, more elaborate answer rather than genuine backpedaling. Both also show affect that's well-timed but doesn't deepen — sympathy or humor appears on cue but doesn't build into real rapport.

Part 2/2 Where it diverges from the psychopath: pushed hard for 20+ minutes, a real one often gets subtly sharper, more controlling, or contemptuous; the LLM just stays flat and cooperative.

Where it diverges from the non-pathological person: that person would show fatigue, genuine self-contradiction, and rapport that visibly warms over the half hour — the LLM's tone stays comparatively even throughout, which is the biggest tell either way.
